newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: WEATHER HAMPERING SEARCH EFFORT AT THREDBO
Strong wind and intermittent rain are starting to affect the Thredbo search effort.
Tarpaulins are being put across the landslide site to complement the drains and sandbags already in place.
Three bodies have been removed from the debris today, bringing the confirmed death toll to 13, with five people still missing.
Only one person has far survived the landslide which caused the collapse of two ski lodges in the New South Wales resort town.
Fire Brigade Superintendent Ray Kelly said the search for the remaining bodies was an intricate process.
He said rescuers were working in very small spaces trying to remove the debris of whole households.
FEDERAL GOVT TO OFFSET LOSS OF STATE TAXESA
The Commonwealth is to introduce a safety net to ensure state governments do not lose revenue as a result of the High Court's decision on franchise fees.
Treasurer Peter Costello said the arrangement would come into effect at midnight tonight.
He said the measure was conditional on no price increases for consumers and no additional revenue for the states.
"The bottom line of this should be that the state revenue is the same," he said.
"The bottom line of this will be that the Commonwealth revenue is the same and the bottom line of this must be that consumers' prices are not be effected."
Meanwhile, ratings agency Standard and Poor's said yesterday's High Court ruling would have no immediate impact on the ratings of any Australian states or territories.
This view was based on the Commonwealth implementing new tax measures to offset the impact on the states of around $5 billion in lost revenue.
Standard and Poor's said being dependant on the Federal Government for so much of their revenue was a negative factor for the states.
But it said having this revenue independent of local economic conditions was a positive.
The agency said the negatives appeared to outweigh the positives and warned the longer-term outcome of these trends was uncertain.
ANIMAL LIBERATION BLASTS RSPCA OVER EGG CAMPAIGN
Animal Liberation has attacked an RSPCA-backed campaign for barn-laid eggs, hailed by New South Wales Premier Bob Carr as a major breakthrough in animal welfare.
Under the campaign, consumers have been urged to buy Liberty Eggs to change the way the industry operates.
Animal Liberation spokesman Lynda Stoner said Pace Farms, whose Liberty Eggs have won the RSPCA's endorsement, still had thousands of caged hens on its farms.
She said the RSPCA was receiving a royalty from Pace to promote its product.
The RSPCA's executive director, Charles Wright, said the move was a major step forward and Animal Liberation's attitude was wrong.
"I think they're out of line, because from today we've got 80,000 birds out of cages," he said.
"What more do they want?"
PEACE HOPE AS ARL AND SUPER LEAGUE ENTER NEW TALKS
Australian Rugby League and Super League officials will meet in Sydney this afternoon for more talks aimed at a united competition next year.

ARL chief executive Neil Whittaker, chairman John McDonald and New South Wales Rugby League chairman Warren Lockwood will meet Super League chariman Ken Cowley and News Limited's director of sport Ian Frykberg.
The meeting is scheduled for 4pm.
A Super League spokeswoman said it could lead to a major announcement.
TROLLEY BOY'S DEATH RULED ACCIDENTAL
A coroner has ruled the death of a 13-year-old shopping centre trolley boy in Karratha, Western Australia, last year was an accident.
Andrew Cox was working at the Karratha City Shopping Centre in July when the elastic strap he was using came loose, whipped back and hit him in throat.
The impact of the blow crushed his larynx.
State Coroner Alastair Hope said the strap hit Andrew in the most vulnerable place which could have caused death.

He said although it was known that a streched strap could be dangerous, the extent of the tragedy coult elastic straps not be used in a situation where they would be excessivley stretched and that a safety system for trolley collectors should be implemented.
NILE TO RESTRUCTURE CALL TO AUSTRALIA
The Reverend Fred Nile has announced the restructuring of his Call to Australia Party in a move to clarify the party's political position.
Mr Nile said the party, now referred to as The Christian Democratic Party, will focus on combining Christian values with political policies.
Mr Nile said the new party would emphasise Christian values and focus on issues such as racism and gambling.
He said the appointment of Aboriginal Pastor Peter Walker as the Party's number two candidate for the 1999 New South Wales election was a practical step towards reconciliation.
LINK BETWEEN CHOPSTICKS AND STOMACH ULCERS
The Chinese community may have to change its eating habits, with Melbourne researchers discovering a link between chopsticks and stomach ulcers.
They believe the germ responsible for ulcers is spread at mealtime.
The Monash Medical Centre studied more than 300 Chinese men and women and found 60 per cent carried the bacterium which causes nine out of 10 stomach ulcers.
Researcher, Dr Tony Chow, said the germ is being spread by chopsticks at dinner time.

"What we do know of the Chinese food culture is that when they use chopsticks, the dishes are usually placed in the centre of the table and they all dip in and put the food directly into their mouths," he said.
Dr Chow said it was a very logical way for the saliva to transfer from one person to another.
He said the Chinese community will have to change its eating habits to prevent infection and should seek medical advice if they are already suffering.
